title: Blue Origin says it is building a higher-performing rocket engine at 1/4 the cost
gist: Blue Origin unveiled Northstar, a BE-4 replacement with half the parts, 30% less mass, 715,000 lbf thrust, and a target cost of 25% of a BE-4, plus a composite hydrogen GS3 third stage that lifts New Glenn's direct-GEO capacity to 8-14 t. The stage is set to debut in 2028 for a government cislunar customer. The company aims eventually for New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.

insights.claim: Blue Origin's Northstar engine, which will replace the BE-4 on New Glenn's first stage, has half the parts, 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent 3D-printable content.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Simpler engine design is central to reusable launch economics and to competing on price with SpaceX.

insights.claim: Blue Origin believes it can build the Northstar engine at 25 percent of the cost of a BE-4 and eventually assemble each engine in less than a day.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Cutting engine cost by 4x and assembling engines in a day would remove manufacturing bottlenecks to high launch cadence.
insights.quote: “To get access to space at a lower cost, we have to look at every part of the vehicle,”
insights.locator: Blue Origin believes it can manufacture

insights.claim: Northstar will start at 715,000 pounds of thrust versus the BE-4's 640,000 pounds, while keeping the methane/liquid oxygen oxygen-rich staged combustion cycle and single-shaft turbopump.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: About 12% more thrust while keeping the proven architecture lowers development risk.
insights.locator: The BE-4 engine powering New Glenn

insights.claim: Blue Origin will continue manufacturing the BE-4 engine for United Launch Alliance, whose Vulcan rocket uses two of them.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: ULA's Vulcan stays dependent on the BE-4, so the Northstar switch does not disrupt ULA supply.
insights.locator: Limp said the company will continue

themes.theme: GS3 hydrogen kick stage expands high-energy market

insights.claim: Blue Origin's GS3 third stage lets New Glenn 7x2 carry 8 metric tons directly to geostationary orbit and 10 tons to translunar injection, rising to 14 and 20 tons for the larger 9x4 variant.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Direct GEO and lunar injection capacity let New Glenn compete for premium high-energy government and commercial missions.
insights.locator: The stage can fly on both

insights.claim: Blue Origin completed its first composite liquid hydrogen tanking test on a 5.5-meter tank, holding 100 percent of maximum operating pressure for 2.5 hours and 150 percent for 10 minutes, overcoming doubts about hydrogen leakage through composites.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Composite hydrogen tanks are hard to build, and this result lowers technical risk for lightweight upper stages.
insights.locator: The company recently had a breakthrough

insights.claim: GS3, powered by the BE-7 engine from Blue Origin's lunar landers, is targeting a 2028 debut for a government customer already signed for a cislunar mission.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A committed government customer reduces demand risk for the new stage.
insights.quote: “We have one customer signed up for cislunar space in 2028,”

insights.claim: Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp says launch demand has never been higher, and the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Management is pricing in a multi-year launch shortage, and its cadence target far exceeds what any rocket flies today.
insights.quote: “There has never been higher demand for launch, ever,”
insights.locator: There has never been higher demand
